meta.title: Who really said "I came, I saw, I conquered"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Julius Caesar really said it. "Veni, vidi, vici" is reported by Suetonius and Plutarch after his 47 BC win at Zela. The real debate is how he said it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I came, I saw, I conquered'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Caesar: reported by Suetonius and Plutarch after his five-day 47 BC victory at Zela. Not a Senate speech — a triumph placard or a terse report home.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Caesar’s. The Latin “veni, vidi, vici” is recorded by Suetonius and, in Greek, by Plutarch, both reporting Caesar’s words after his lightning victory over Pharnaces II at Zela in 47 BC. The familiar English “I came, I saw, I conquered” is the standard rendering, found verbatim in Alexander Thomson’s public-domain translation.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Victory over Pharnaces II at Zela, 47 BC

source.excerpt: In his Pontic triumph he displayed among the show-pieces of the procession a tablet with the three words “veni, vidi, vici” — not signifying, like the rest, what was done, but how swiftly it was finished.
trail: Three ancient authors record the line: Appian ties it to a letter to the Senate, Plutarch to a report sent to a friend in Rome, and Suetonius to a placard carried in Caesar’s Pontic triumph.
The occasion was Caesar’s crushing five-day defeat of Pharnaces II of Pontus at Zela in 47 BC; the phrase marked the war’s speed, not its spoils.
Plutarch gives the Greek “ἤλθον, εἶδον, ἐνίκησα”; the three-word Latin “veni, vidi, vici” is preserved by Suetonius and cited in Wikiquote’s sourced section.
source.excerptNote: Paraphrasing Suetonius, Divus Julius 37. Plutarch instead reports the words in a message Caesar sent to Rome; the sources agree on the wording, not the medium.

sourceLink.text: Suetonius, Life of Julius Caesar, ch. 37 (Wikisource)

source.rightsNote: Caesar’s words (47 BC) and the ancient accounts of Suetonius (c. AD 121) and Plutarch are far older than any copyright term. The exact English wording “I came, I saw, I conquered” appears in Alexander Thomson’s translation of Suetonius (first published 1761, revised 1855) — also long in the public domain.

author.name: Julius Caesar
author.heading: About Julius Caesar
author.bio: Gaius Julius Caesar (100–44 BC) was a Roman general and politician whose conquest of Gaul and victory in the civil war made him dictator of Rome. A noted prose stylist, he wrote his own Commentaries on those wars; the clipped, self-promoting economy of “veni, vidi, vici” is very much in that voice. He was assassinated in the Senate on the Ides of March, 44 BC.

misattribution.heading: The real story
misattribution.intro: The author is not in doubt — but almost everything people add about how Caesar said it is shakier than the confident retellings suggest.

items.why: Only Appian links it to a letter to the Senate. Suetonius says it was an inscription on a placard in his triumph, and Plutarch that it was a terse note to a friend named Amantius. The ancient sources genuinely disagree.

items.who: “Caesar said ‘I came, I saw, I conquered’”
items.why: He said it in Latin — “veni, vidi, vici” — three words whose alliteration and clipped rhythm are the whole point; the English is a faithful but flatter rendering. Plutarch even notes the phrase’s assonance in Greek.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are authentically Caesar’s, reported independently by Suetonius and Plutarch — a rare case where a famous ancient one-liner survives the fact-check intact.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Caesar’s war against Pharnaces II of Pontus was over almost before it began: he reached the field at Zela and destroyed the enemy within five days of his arrival, and in about four hours of actual fighting. The boast’s power lies in its economy — three words, each two syllables, each beginning with the same sound — mirroring the speed of the campaign itself.

According to Suetonius the phrase was not meant to list what Caesar had won but to advertise how fast he had won it. That self-conscious brevity is why the line outlived the battle and became shorthand, for two thousand years, for effortless total victory.
detailsBody: Modern classicists treat the wording as authentic while remaining agnostic about its medium. A 2013 study in The Classical Quarterly (“Veni Vidi Vici and Caesar’s Triumph”) reviews the conflicting testimony of Appian, Plutarch and Suetonius and argues the placard in the Pontic triumph is the most historically grounded setting.
Whether or not Caesar personally coined it on the spot, all surviving accounts attribute the words to him and none to anyone else — which is why this sits at ‘verified’ rather than ‘attributed.’
context.pull: Three words, one for each stage of a war that lasted five days.
